summary: Describes the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the Internet Architecture Board. It is a periodic status list. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1800.

plainLanguage.summary: A report card showing how official each internet rule had become.

subtitle: The Internet Architecture Board's map of protocol standardization status.

tldr.problem: The Internet needed a way to categorize and track protocols as they progressed through development, testing, and deployment stages, and to communicate their standardization status to implementers.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board publishes this periodic list organizing all Internet protocols by their maturity level (standard, draft standard, proposed standard, experimental, informational, historic) and their requirement level (required, recommended, elective, limited use, not recommended) for different types of systems.
tldr.outcome: This document became the official reference for understanding which protocols should be implemented in which systems, and has itself become historic as replaced by RFC 1800.

facts.label: Requirement levels defined
facts.value: 5 (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended)

today: RFC 1780 is historic and was replaced by RFC 1800. It served as a periodic snapshot of protocol standardization status during the early Internet era, helping implementers understand the maturity and applicability of protocols for different system types.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1780 describes the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet as determined by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB). It was published in March 1995 as an Internet Standard itself (STD 1) and is intended to be issued approximately quarterly as a snapshot of the current status of all Internet protocols.

The RFC explains how the Internet community tracks protocol development: from early proposals through increasingly rigorous stages of testing and deployment, until a protocol becomes an official standard or is declared historic. It also defines a separate dimension: the requirement level of each protocol for different types of systems.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is like a progress report on all the internet rules, showing which ones are official standards and which are still being tested.

sections.title: Maturity Levels and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
RFC 1780 defines two independent dimensions for categorizing protocols. The maturity level describes the state of standardization: Standard means the IESG has established it as official; Draft Standard means it is under active consideration with substantial testing desired; Proposed Standard may be considered in the future; Experimental protocols are for ongoing research not intended for operational use; Informational documents describe protocols from other organizations; and Historic protocols are superseded or unused.

The requirement level describes how broadly a protocol should be implemented: Required must be implemented in all systems; Recommended systems should implement; Elective systems may or may not implement; Limited Use for specialized circumstances; and Not Recommended for general use. These two dimensions are independent, so a standard protocol might be elective, and a proposed protocol might be recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols are rated two ways: how tested they are (from experimental to standard) and how important it is to use them (from required to not recommended).

sections.title: The Standards Track Process
sections.content:
The RFC describes the progression protocols follow on the standards track. A protocol enters as a Proposed Standard only with IESG recommendation. It must remain proposed standard for at least six months before advancing to Draft Standard, which requires at least two independent implementations and IESG approval. After at least four more months as a draft standard, a protocol can be promoted to full Standard status, which requires operational experience and demonstrated interoperability.

Off-track states are also defined: protocols may be moved to Experimental when they are not ready for standardization, or to Historic when they are superseded or abandoned. This measured progression, with mandatory waiting periods and multiple implementation requirements, ensures that Internet standards are thoroughly tested before official adoption.
sections.plainLanguage: New protocols go through stages like a school: they propose themselves, wait six months, become draft standards, wait four months more, then finally become full standards once proven to work.

sections.title: Organization of Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC organizes Internet protocols into separate lists by maturity level, containing sections for Standard Protocols, Draft Standard Protocols, Proposed Standard Protocols, Telnet Options (a special category), Experimental Protocols, Informational Protocols, Historic Protocols, and Obsolete Protocols. For each, it lists the protocol name, its requirement level, the relevant RFC number, and often an STD number (assigned to standard protocols).

Notable standard protocols listed include the core Internet suite: IP, TCP, UDP, ICMP, IGMP, SMTP, DNS, SNMP, and others. The document also includes sections on network-specific standards (how to run IP over particular physical networks like Ethernet) and applicability statements explaining how certain protocols should be used in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sorts all the protocols like a library catalog, with shelves for official standards, drafts, experiments, and old retired rules.

sections.title: Historical Status
sections.content:
RFC 1780 is a historic document that captured a snapshot of Internet protocol standards in March 1995. It is no longer the official list; it was superseded by RFC 1800 and subsequent standards lists.

The RFC illustrates the Internet standards process as it existed in the mid-1990s, before the broader Internet population and the rise of web technologies transformed standardization practices. It remains valuable as a historical reference for understanding how the Internet standardization machinery worked during the early protocol era, when TCP/IP, DNS, SMTP, and the core protocols were still maturing.
sections.plainLanguage: This list is now outdated, replaced by newer ones, but it shows how the Internet kept track of its rules back in 1995.
